item.title: A Maowusu reunion rooted in American's kindness, forged by Chinese farmer's grit
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Yin Yuzhen (L), Bai Wanxiang (R) and Ronald Sakolsky pose for a photo with a tree they once planted together in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 24, 2026. Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky revisited the Maowusu Sandy Land on Monday and planted sapling with his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees here for four decades, as well as Yin's husband Bai Wanxiang. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) HOHHOT, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- For more than a quarter of a century, a retired American teacher and a Chinese woman fighting desertification have lived on opposite sides of the Pacific, bound together by old photos, a newspaper and a forest. On Sunday, they finally met again, face to face. As Ronald Sakolsky descended an escalator at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, he wiped tears from his eyes with his right hand while clutching a bouquet in his left. At the bottom stood Yin Yuzhen, a woman who has spent over four decades wringing green life from the Maowusu, the fourth-largest sandy area in China. The short ride down the escalator was the last stretch before their long-awaited embrace, 26 years after their first in-person meeting. Their friendship began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province -- more than 11,000 kilometers from his home in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries. One ordinary evening, a television program caught his eye. On the screen was Yin, planting trees to help hold back the advancing sands of the Maowusu sandy land. Stretching across parts of Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and Ningxia, the Maowusu has been one of the front lines in China's fight against desertification in the north: an effort launched in 1978 and slated to continue through 2050. But for Yin, the fight against the sand was not an abstract national effort. In those years, a night of strong winds could leave the doorway of their dugout sealed by sand. There was grit in the food, dirt in the water, and little else in sight but miles of shifting yellow stretching in every direction. By 1999, Yin had planted trees across some 30,000 mu (about 2,000 hectares) of barren land -- an area equivalent to around 2,800 standard soccer pitches. "I was so touched that I started to cry," Sakolsky recalled, thinking back to that evening. "I honestly cannot tell you why. Something just happened to me. I just felt like I needed to help." Over the next two months, he contacted more than a dozen organizations across the United States. A Boston-based charity agreed to provide a grant of 5,000 U.S. dollars. At the time, the donation was a staggering sum for Yin -- enough to build a house, cover the costs of raising her children, and give her family a very different life. Yet, Yin spent it all on saplings, keeping only a single banknote as a memento. In May 2000, Sakolsky took a train from Luoyang, Henan, and then switched to another vehicle, jolting all the way into the sandy land to see the saplings with his own eyes. He later described the landscape as desolate: "No roads, no trees, no houses. We were just driving over one dune after another." Then he spotted Yin. "She popped out of a hole," Sakolsky said. The two couldn't speak each other's language, and they relied entirely on gestures and smiles to communicate. Yin showed Sakolsky how to plant. To Sakolsky, the saplings looked so fragile that he thought they might never grow much higher than his knees. Deep down, he could not see how this patch of sand could ever become a forest. He told her so plainly: "This is impossible." That night, Yin and her husband invited him to their home for dinner, and made him a steaming bowl of noodles. "Delicious," Sakolsky recalled. Sakolsky went home months later, and they lost touch. Across the Pacific, he kept telling his students about the Chinese woman who was trying to turn a desert green. In China, whenever Yin met an American, she would pull out an old photograph of Sakolsky and ask if they knew how she could get in touch with him. RECONNECTED ONLINE Year after year, her search went nowhere, until a video and a social media post achieved what years of searching had not. In May this year, Yin stood before the forest she had spent decades growing, holding up the old dollar bill -- the one she had saved from the money Sakolsky had raised. She looked into the camera and said: "Mr. Sakolsky, if you see this video, I invite you to come back to China and see the forest that grew from the money you sent us." The appeal quickly went viral online. Within hours, messages began reaching Sakolsky in the form of emails and texts from strangers telling him that a Chinese woman was looking for him. Less than 26 hours after Yin posted the video, they found him. The two then reconnected online. This was followed by photographs and videos. For the first time, Sakolsky saw what had become of the saplings he had once thought too small to make much difference: a forest of more than 50,000 trees. "Amazing. Absolutely amazing," he said. A DREAM FULFILLED Upon arriving in Beijing early this past Sunday, Sakolsky received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the sandy land. He flew to Ordos that afternoon. "This is a dream come true from a lady who is the hero of the story," he told media gathered around them at the local airport. "I never thought I would see her again," Sakolsky said. For him, this visit brought home the power of a culture that lives by its promises. Yin had vowed that the saplings would take root and grow, and that one day he could come back to see them for himself. Today, including the trees funded by Sakolsky's efforts, Yin and her family have planted trees across 70,000 mu, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Poplars, oriental arborvitaes, spruce and Mongolian Scots pines now rustle in the wind as birds chirp. Official figures show that about 85 percent of the Maowusu has been restored. Between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and managed to rehabilitate approximately 152 million mu of sandified land. When he raised the money in 1999, he expected nothing in return, Sakolsky said. "You can't give something and then expect something back," he told Xinhua. "I raised that money because I wanted to thank China, and I wanted to help her make China a little more beautiful. That's all." On Monday afternoon, Sakolsky walked through a carpet of fallen leaves as Yin led him to a tall, sturdy poplar, more than 10 meters high, in a grove named in his honor. He could hardly believe it. This was the tree he and Yin had planted together 26 years ago. Back then, the sapling had been no thicker than a finger, swaying in the wind as if it might be swallowed by the sand at any moment. Yin handed him a shovel. "Let's plant another one." The two bent down together. Yin steadied the sapling as Sakolsky pressed soil around its roots -- his hands trembling slightly but his movements steady. "I planted a friendship tree in Inner Mongolia," Sakolsky said. FRIENDSHIP FOR GENERATIONS To welcome Sakolsky, more than a dozen members of Yin's family had come from different places to be there for the meeting. Red chili peppers hung by the doorway and small pumpkins lined the walls, while the courtyard had been swept clean. "I asked my children to come back because I hope the friendship between our two families will last for generations," Yin said. "I want my children and grandchildren to remember it." For Sakolsky, the reunion with Yin and her family is about more than a forest. It is a reminder that no act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted. Given time, a small act can take root, spread and grow into something no one could have imagined. The story of Sakolsky and Yin adds another thread to the long history of goodwill between the people of China and the United States -- from the American volunteer pilots who fought alongside Chinese forces during World War II to the historic visit of a U.S. table tennis team to China in 1971 and, more recently, the Philadelphia Orchestra's decades of performances in the country. During his stay in China from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1, Sakolsky will also take part in China-U.S. teacher exchanges and return to Henan, where he will meet teachers and students at the school where he once taught, among other activities. The retired history teacher believes that while people may look different and come from different cultures, underneath it all, everyone bleeds red. "Whether you're Chinese or American, we all love our families, we all love life, and we all love the Earth," he said. Americans and Chinese need to "focus on our similarities and not on our differences," he once noted. He hopes that when the trip is over, the message can reach people around the world: Chinese and American people "can work together and make a peaceful world." "I see where the United States and China can work together," said Sakolsky. "So I will not quit. She never quit. 'Quit' is not in her vocabulary. Together, it works." ■ Ronald Sakolsky (R), Yin Yuzhen (L) and Bai Wanxiang plant a sapling in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 24, 2026. item.title: U.S. threatens "economic D-Day" sanctions on Iran
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
NEW YORK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday threatened Iran with "an economic D-Day," announcing a wave of new sanctions aimed at further isolating the country. "We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe," said Bessent at a press conference. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline" that sustains the country, he said. The U.S. Treasury Department said in a press release that the new sectoral sanctions determinations target five critical sectors -- digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping -- that the U.S. says Iran has relied on to prop up its economy. The measures marked the beginning of "a sustained and systematic campaign to close every financial resource" that supports Iran, the department said. It added that "any entity that facilitates money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system." The department is expanding the categories of "Iran-related conduct" that the United States might sanction in the future, and said "every country will be given a defined timeline to shut down the Iran-related activity" the United States has identified. Bessent disclosed that U.S. President Donald Trump has been calling world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with Iran. Simultaneously, the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that enable Iran's activities, including illicit nuclear and missile technology procurement, cyber operations, and oil-revenue generation networks. OFAC also suspended several general licenses that previously authorized certain remittance payments to Iran and Iranian access to the U.S. cultural and academic system. Additionally, the Treasury Department released additional guidance on the sanctions risks associated with complying with Iranian demands regarding shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. In a post on X, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf responded to U.S. economic threats against Tehran by saying that, "Iran's trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don't take these statements into account anywhere." "They cannot cut off our financial lifelines," Iran's Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance Seyed Ali Madanizadeh said in another X post, adding that Tehran has been "planning for some time to counter the sanctions." ■

item.title: China proposes formulating at least 100 key standards for humanoid robots by 2028
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China has proposed formulating at least 100 key standards for the humanoid robot industry by 2028, according to a draft guideline from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The draft guideline for developing a national standard system for the humanoid robot industry will be open for public comment from Aug. 25 to Sept. 23. The proposed standards would cover areas including methods for capability testing and evaluation, key technologies, platforms and systems, application scenarios and safety governance. By 2028, the draft also aims to establish a systematic, science-based and coordinated standard system, with more than 200 enterprises promoting and implementing these standards. Humanoid robots are defined in the draft as a new generation of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven intelligent terminals with human-like forms and capabilities that can autonomously perform complex tasks. Rapid development of the sector has created an urgent need for common standards covering terminology, interfaces, testing and evaluation to guide technological innovation, product development and large-scale application, according to the draft. More than 100 humanoid robot-related standards are already under development or preliminary research in China and abroad. The draft calls for standardizing methodologies for grading humanoid robot capabilities. It also proposes standardizing the definition of unique identifiers, coding rules and identification mechanisms for humanoid robots. For industrial applications, the draft proposes requirements covering operational capabilities and environmental adaptability for humanoid robots working in structured and semi-structured industrial environments. The push for standards comes as China steps up efforts to deploy humanoid robots in real-world settings. In June, the MIIT and China's state assets regulator launched a training initiative targeting application validation and regular deployment in representative scenarios by the end of 2026, as well as deployment capacity at the 10,000-unit scale. At a July 20 press briefing, the MIIT said China had developed more than 400 humanoid robot models, over half of the global total. Common interfaces and safety standards are also emerging as practical issues in industrial deployment. Industrial production leaves little room for error. Reflections and dust can disrupt perception, while continuous operation places heavy demands on durability, heat management and component life. Beyond technical and industrial specifications, the draft calls for standards governing ethical requirements and social-impact assessments in the development and application of humanoid robot technologies, placing safety and ethics alongside performance and commercialization in the proposed standards system. The framework will be developed under the principles of being systematic and comprehensive, prioritizing urgent needs, and allowing for dynamic updates, according to the draft. ■

item.title: 2026 APEC SME ministerial meeting to focus on innovation, cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The 32nd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Ministerial Meeting will be held on Sept. 4 in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) said on Monday. The meeting, themed "innovation-driven development for win-win cooperation," will bring together SME officials from APEC economies, representatives of the APEC Secretariat, and other guests. The meeting will focus on technological innovation, digital empowerment and inclusive development, with a joint ministerial statement and other outcome documents expected, according to Liang Zhifeng, director of the SME bureau under the MIIT. As the host, China hopes that through in-depth exchanges, all economies will reach forward-looking and practical consensus, promote mutual learning of policies and the translation of outcomes, and jointly enhance the innovation capacity, digitalization level and sustainable development capabilities of SMEs in the Asia-Pacific region, said Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology Ke Jixin. Wang Sheng, vice governor of Guangdong, said that all preparations for the meeting are essentially complete, and all APEC economies had confirmed their participation. More than 2,100 companies from home and abroad have registered for the accompanying exhibitions, with over 3,900 booths planned. China will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in south China in November this year, which will mark the country's third hosting of the event following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. This year marks the APEC "China Year," with the theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." Approximately 300 APEC-related meetings and events will take place in multiple Chinese cities throughout the year. ■

item.title: Chinese film turns kitchen into anti-war statement
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
*The film is set in the Middle East, but its emotional center lies elsewhere: in the universal desire to live an ordinary life. *"Don't forget to eat well" is an ordinary phrase in peaceful times. In the film, it becomes something much larger -- a reminder of the normal life that war threatens to take away. *In the movie, the restaurant becomes a small refuge: water, electricity, food, and people from different backgrounds sharing a table while the outside world is held at bay. by Xinhua writers Zhang Yunlong, Xing Tuo and Xiong Jialin BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Xu Fu and Ma Junsheng are asleep when a blast wakes them and for a moment, they think it is an earthquake. Then comes the shockwave, and the understanding that war has arrived. The pivotal scene in Chinese film "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" turns a restaurant kitchen into the center of a story about war, survival and peace. Directed and co-written by Wen Muye, the film follows Xu Fu, a Chinese cook who travels to the Middle East to work in a Chinese restaurant after falling into debt at home. He and restaurant manager Ma Junsheng help build a popular eatery that becomes a gathering place for people of different backgrounds. Then war breaks out. The film opened in Chinese mainland cinemas on Aug. 11. Maoyan, a Chinese ticketing platform, forecasts that the film could gross more than 2.5 billion yuan (about 369 million U.S. dollars) in the Chinese mainland, after it had already taken in around 1.6 billion yuan by Monday. The film has also received a rating of 8.6 on Douban, a major review platform. The film's appeal lies less in its explosion scenes, than in what happens between them. WHY FOOD Wen said the decision to tell a war story through a restaurant came from a simple contrast: war is cruel, while food represents happiness. The film returns repeatedly to cooking, from dumplings prepared before Xu leaves home to a wedding banquet where Chinese and Arab food traditions meet. Later, fleeing the fighting with a group of orphaned children, Xu prepares a simple pot of rice. The meal is modest, Wen said, but it gives the children a sense of safety. The dish eventually becomes known as "Xu Fu Rice Stew" at the restaurant. The film is set in the Middle East, but its emotional center lies elsewhere: in the universal desire to live an ordinary life. "Don't forget to eat well" is an ordinary phrase in peaceful times. In the film, it becomes something much larger -- a reminder of the normal life that war threatens to take away. RESTAURANT IN RUINS The restaurant setting reflects a familiar reality in the history of Chinese migration. For decades, opening restaurants has been one of the most common ways for Chinese migrants to make a living overseas. The film's Loong Restaurant is rooted in a real story. Shuai Xuejun, from Jiangxi Province, traveled to Iraq in 2004 at age 31 and opened a restaurant of the same name with friends in Baghdad, in a run-down building with broken windows and no proper door. The restaurant eventually grew into a thriving business, employing about 20 people and generating daily revenue of 4,000 to 5,000 U.S. dollars at its peak. But the noise of the restaurant could not keep out the war. One morning, Shuai was woken by a blast that shook dust loose from the walls; the bomb had exploded about three kilometers away. What stayed with him the longest, he said, was not the sound of explosions but small acts of kindness. A regular customer helped him replace a malfunctioning television for recreation when the store was closed during the war. When Shuai finally left Iraq in March 2005, another regular customer told him: "When you leave, there will be no Chinese flavor here." Shuai and his colleagues later wrote a book about their experiences. A film company acquired the rights years later. MORE THAN FOOD The film resonates with the people who have lived through war themselves. Ahmed Mohammed Jaber Alkalthoom, an Iraqi-born actor who appears briefly in the film, is better known in China as a food blogger. Born in Iraq in 1994, Jaber grew up amid conflict. He later recalled once mistaking the sound of missiles for fireworks. He moved to China with his family in 2014 and began filming Chinese food in 2018. In 2024, while filming a video during the Chinese New Year holiday, he froze at the sound of a firecracker. "I thought it was a bomb," he recalled. Viewers who saw the footage left messages reassuring him: "Don't be afraid. This is China." "During wartime, there would be no water or electricity. A family would take out the food they had hidden and share it, and that felt warm and healing," he said. For him, being able to eat well became part of everyday Chinese life -- something he still regards as "a great thing." WAR STORY WITHOUT SUPER HERO The film also stands apart from more conventional action-driven war stories. Xu Fu is not a conventional hero. Going abroad to earn money and pay off debt, he is an ordinary man whose life is gradually transformed as the war forces him to confront the fate of those around him. Ma Junsheng, who is more idealistic, ultimately sacrifices himself protecting children. Saif, an orphan who initially steals food to survive, gradually learns to cook under Xu's guidance. Egyptian journalist Mohamed Mazen, who has lived in China for 17 years, said he did not feel the usual distance he associates with Chinese cinema while watching the film. Its questions about war, food and ordinary life, he said, cross cultural boundaries. Mazen said he was struck by the film's perspective on war. Having grown up watching Hollywood films, he was accustomed to stories centered on soldiers, rescuers and larger-than-life heroes. In contrast, he said, "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" focuses on cooks, restaurant workers and children trying to preserve a sense of normality amid violence. In the movie, the restaurant becomes a small refuge: water, electricity, food, and people from different backgrounds sharing a table while the outside world is held at bay. Years later, Xu Fu returns to the region as a tourist. Finding the Loong Restaurant again, he discovers that Saif, the orphan who he once taught to cook, has become its head chef. The boy who grew up in war has chosen a life in the kitchen, with a spatula in his hand rather than a gun -- a quiet ending to a film that measures the cost of war not only in lives lost, but in the ordinary life people struggle to preserve. (Video reporter: Xu Haofu, Yao Bing, Dong Xiuzhu and Zhang Yanfang; video editors: Liang Wanshan, Roger Lott and Zheng Qingbin)■

item.title: Xi calls on China, Jordan to further deepen alignment of development strategies
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein, who is on a state visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang) BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China and Jordan should further deepen the alignment of development strategies, Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Monday. Both sides should enhance cooperation in traditional fields including economy and trade, infrastructure construction, transportation and mining, expand new drivers of cooperation in digital economy, artificial intelligence and green energy, and comprehensively deepen exchanges in education, culture, science and technology, tourism and other areas, Xi said when holding talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in Beijing. Xi noted that in 2015, the two heads of state jointly announced the establishment of China-Jordan strategic partnership, opening a new chapter in the development of bilateral relations. Facing an international and regional situation characterized by intertwined changes and chaos, building a more substantive and dynamic China-Jordan relationship is in line with the common expectations of the two peoples and also conforms to the general trend of the pursuit of the Global South for strength through unity, he said. Xi emphasized that China attaches great importance to Jordan's unique and significant role in the region, firmly supports Jordan in safeguarding its national sovereignty, security and development interests, and is willing to maintain close exchanges with Jordan at all levels including the governments, political parties, legislative bodies and localities, and enhance exchanges of experience in governance. China is willing to work with Jordan to implement the four major global initiatives, enhance coordination and cooperation in multilateral institutions including the United Nations, jointly safeguard the international system with the United Nations at its core and the international order underpinned by international law, and promote the building of a community with a shared future for humanity, Xi said. King Abdullah II said Jordan and China have established a strong strategic partnership, with fruitful cooperation across various fields. He said Jordan firmly upholds the one-China policy and regards Taiwan as part of China's territory. Jordan places high priority on its relations with China and is dedicated to expanding cooperation and exchanges in economy and trade, manufacturing, agriculture, science and technology, pharmaceuticals, culture and education, King Abdullah II said, adding that Jordan welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest there to achieve common development and prosperity. Jordan speaks highly of the four global initiatives put forward by President Xi and looks forward to China's greater leading role on the global stage, King Abdullah II said. After the talks, the two heads of state jointly attended a signing ceremony for multiple cooperation documents in areas such as diplomacy, economy and trade, industrial and supply chains, and justice. The two sides also issued a joint statement on deepening the strategic partnership between China and Jordan. Prior to the talks in the Great Hall of the People, Xi held a welcome ceremony for King Abdullah II. Xi also hosted a welcome banquet for him in the evening. ■ Chinese President Xi Jinping holds a welcome ceremony for King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in the Northern Hall of the Great Hall of the People prior to their talks in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 24, 2026. item.title: Xi puts forward four principles on Palestinian question
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein, who is on a state visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang) BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping stressed on Monday that four principles should be followed to push for the resolution of the Palestinian question, which is at the heart of the Middle East issue. Xi made the remarks in talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in Beijing. First, a political settlement should be upheld. The two-state solution is the right direction, and efforts should be made to restart peace talks between Palestine and Israel, with a view to establishing an independent Palestinian state at an early date, Xi said. Second, the principle of "Palestinians governing Palestine" should be followed in advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-war reconstruction of Gaza, he said. Third, humanitarian principles must be upheld. The international community, and the UN Security Council in particular, should shoulder its responsibility effectively to protect civilian safety, ensure the flow of humanitarian assistance, and put an end to humanitarian disasters, Xi said. Fourth, fairness and justice must be upheld. This means following international law, addressing both symptoms and root causes, and taking practical actions so that the Palestinian question can be resolved in a comprehensive, just and lasting way at an early date, he said. On the Middle East situation, Xi said China has always advocated a comprehensive ceasefire and end of hostilities, and resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, adding that the sovereignty and security of Jordan and all other countries in the region should be respected. Noting Jordan appreciates China's impartial stance on Middle East affairs and its support for the just cause of Arab countries, King Abdullah II said Jordan is ready to maintain close communication with China and continue to make active efforts for de-escalation. ■

item.title: Xi stresses consolidating, expanding campaign on correct view of governance performance
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, has emphasized the importance of consolidating and expanding the progress made in a Party-wide study and education campaign for establishing and practicing a correct understanding of governance performance. Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was studied at a meeting of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building held on Monday. Xi stressed that establishing and putting into practice a correct view of governance performance is a long-term task that requires sustained efforts. Since the 18th CPC National Congress, the organization of study and education campaigns across the Party to address major and pressing issues in Party building has become an important institutional arrangement, Xi said, lauding the notable results achieved in the latest campaign. Xi emphasized the need to regularly conduct education on the correct view of governance performance, guiding Party members and officials to always take responsibility, perform their duties and fulfill their obligations in accordance with such a view. Efforts should also be made to improve differentiated assessment and evaluation systems, and establish a personnel selection and appointment orientation that values solid work and concrete results, Xi said. During the meeting, participants thoroughly studied and implemented Xi's instruction, reviewed the campaign, and made arrangements for consolidating and expanding the campaign's outcomes and establishing a long-term mechanism accordingly. The meeting was chaired by Cai Qi, who is head of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building, and was also attended by Li Xi, the group's deputy head. Cai and Li, both of whom are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, also delivered speeches. The meeting noted that the campaign has resolved prominent issues related to deviations in view of governance performance, regulated the official conduct of leading officials at all levels, and given a strong boost to all work aimed at ensuring a good start to the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The campaign, which started in late February, has basically concluded and aimed to correct misguided views on governance that often breed vanity projects, hidden risks, heavy burdens on local communities, and public discontent. ■
